source.title: Flatness is Necessary, Neural Collapse is Not: Rethinking Generalization via Grokking
source.authors: Ting-Xu Han; Linara Adilova; Henning Petzka; J. Kleesiek; Michael Kamp

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The paper has an internal model-name inconsistency for the CIFAR-10 relative-flatness experiment: Section 6 says ResNet-10, while Appendix C.2 describes ResNet-18.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether a relative-flatness measure tracks held-out performance and whether regularizing toward sharper solutions delays generalization. It uses a different measure and intervention from the version’s specified magnitude-aware perturbation comparison.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking timing, neural-collapse regularization, and relative-flatness regularization. Only the relative-flatness results bear on V7; random-label memorization, width sweeps, and the other listed conditions are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study investigates generalization using a penultimate-layer, weight-norm-weighted Hessian measure and interventions that maximize it. It does not measure V7's tolerance to magnitude-scaled weight perturbations or compare that measure's ranking with norm- and margin-based measures. Its own results do not test V1–V8 as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors argue that relative flatness is potentially necessary for generalization under representative-feature and locally constant-label assumptions, whereas neural collapse is unnecessary. They report impaired generalization under sharpness-promoting regularization and recovery after its removal with additional recipe changes. Their stronger causal and necessity language exceeds what these confounded interventions alone establish.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a penultimate-layer relative-flatness metric and regularization interventions; it does not reproduce the version’s weight-perturbation comparison or ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Regularization strength and weight cap affect stability and validation performance; removing the regularizer is paired with changes to learning rate, schedule, and weight decay. Seed-dependent minima and validation accuracy are noted.

fits_no_version.finding: Maximizing the numerical relative-flatness measure maintains sharper solutions and lowers validation accuracy despite nearly perfect training accuracy: approximately 78% to 60% on CIFAR-10, 42% to 38% on ImageNet-100, 44% to 38% for TinyBERT, and 45% to 37% for DistilGPT2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A penultimate-layer Hessian-based relative-flatness intervention can impair held-out accuracy while preserving training accuracy in the tested classification settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation accuracy recovers toward baseline after regularizer removal together with feature-normalization and optimization changes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A combined change to geometric regularization and the training recipe can restore held-out accuracy after sharpness-promoting training.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix C.2 reports that lambda = 0.001 maintains high relative-flatness values with near-baseline validation accuracy; weight cap 20 yields approximately 75% versus 78% baseline accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relationship between this Hessian-based relative-flatness measure and validation accuracy depends on regularizer strength and weight constraints.

record.problems: Relative-flatness regularization results are not a clean isolated intervention: recovery also changes the learning-rate schedule and weight decay. The paper reports means and divergence on plots and uses three seeds for several experiments, but does not state numerical uncertainty for the extracted validation values. CIFAR-10 model naming differs between Section 6 and Appendix C.2. Conclusions are limited to classification and generative language model settings; the authors note assumptions about representative features and locally constant labels.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. The grokking timing and neural-collapse regularization results concern properties not named by V1–V8; the paper's other reported outcomes do not directly measure those versions.

untested.parts: Natural-label versus fixed-random-label fitting and held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Held-out performance with versus without dropout; disabling dropout throughout does not test its effect.
The association between magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance and generalization gaps among comparably fitted convolutional networks, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The extracted accuracy differences are not partial observations of V7. Untested measurement and ranking requirements do not warrant limits_scope labels. Smaller numerical values of the study's relative-flatness measure indicate flatter solutions.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare natural labels with fixed random labels or test held-out performance under random-label training.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.

Does not test the specified magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation measure, rank it against norm- and margin-based measures, or test the cited sharpness counterexamples. Its results use relative flatness and regularization interventions.
Does not identify and remove memorized examples.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Regularized training that maximizes relative flatness; compare validation accuracy with standard training.
rows.note: The appendix describes ResNet-18; Section 6 calls the CIFAR-10 model ResNet-10. Training accuracy approaches 100% in both conditions.
rows.check: The approximately 78% versus 60% validation accuracies are correctly reported, but concern a different sharpness measure and cannot establish V7. Maximizing the numerical relative-flatness measure encourages sharpness. Appendix C.2 identifies ResNet-18; Section 6 inconsistently says ResNet-10.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Remove the relative-flatness regularizer and continue training with learning-rate reset, cosine schedule, and weight decay.
rows.note: Recovery also changes the learning-rate schedule and adds weight decay.
rows.check: Recovery toward 78% is reported, but does not measure V7's perturbation tolerance. Removal also deactivates feature normalization, resets the learning rate, adds cosine scheduling, and introduces weight decay; weight capping remains active.

rows.subject: ViT-tiny
rows.operation_detail: Regularized training that maximizes relative flatness; compare validation accuracy with standard training.
rows.note: Training accuracy approaches 100% in both conditions; relative flatness remains above 20,000 with regularization.
rows.check: Appendix C.3 reports approximately 42% versus 38% validation accuracy; Section 6 gives approximately 43% as optimal. The Hessian-based measure differs from V7's perturbation tolerance, and ViT-tiny is outside its convolutional-family comparison.

rows.subject: ViT-tiny
rows.operation_detail: Remove the relative-flatness regularizer and continue training with learning-rate reset, cosine schedule, and weight decay.
rows.note: Recovery also changes the learning-rate schedule and adds weight decay.
rows.check: Recovery toward 42% is reported, but cannot establish V7. Removal also changes feature normalization, learning rate, scheduling, and weight decay.

rows.subject: TinyBERT
rows.operation_detail: Regularized fine-tuning that maximizes relative flatness; compare validation accuracy with standard fine-tuning.
rows.note: Training accuracy reaches 100% with regularization; relative flatness remains above 700.
rows.check: The approximately 44% versus 38% validation accuracies are correctly reported. TinyBERT fine-tuning on SST-5 with a Hessian-based regularizer does not measure V7's specified behavior in convolutional networks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-10, ImageNet-100, and SST-5 experiments with relative-flatness regularization and subsequent removal
reader_labels.reason: Regularization that maintains high relative flatness coincides with lower validation accuracy, while removing it alongside other training changes restores validation accuracy toward baseline (R1–R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The results support a relationship under these settings, but do not establish the specified magnitude-scaled perturbation ranking or isolate flatness from accompanying training changes during recovery (R1–R8).
